topics.name: Periodic and Oscillatory Motion: Displacement as a Function of Time
topics.summary: A periodic motion repeats itself after equal intervals of time; an oscillatory motion is a periodic motion that goes to and fro about a fixed mean position. The time for one complete repetition is the period \( T \), and the number of repetitions per second is the frequency \( f=1/T \), measured in hertz. In simple harmonic motion the displacement is a sinusoidal function of time, \( x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi) \) or equivalently a cosine form. Here \( A \) is the amplitude (the maximum displacement from the mean position), \( \omega=2\pi f=2\pi/T \) is the angular frequency in rad/s, the full argument \( (\omega t+\phi) \) is the phase, and \( \phi \) is the phase constant that fixes where the motion starts. Starting at the mean position gives a sine with zero phase constant; release from rest at an extreme gives a cosine. SHM can also be seen as the projection of uniform circular motion onto a diameter: the radius becomes the amplitude and the revolution frequency becomes the oscillation frequency.
topics.worked_example:
A particle moves as \( x=6\cos(\pi t/3) \) cm. Find its period and its displacement at \( t=2 \) s.

\( \omega=\pi/3 \) rad/s, so \( T=2\pi/(\pi/3)=6 \) s.

At \( t=2 \) s the phase is \( 2\pi/3 \), and \( \cos(2\pi/3)=-\tfrac12 \), so \( x=-3 \) cm.
common_mistakes: Using \( f \) where \( \omega \) is needed, silently dropping the \( 2\pi \) factor
Treating period and frequency as the same quantity instead of reciprocals
Reporting the extreme-to-extreme distance \( 2A \) as the amplitude
Forgetting to include the phase constant when evaluating the phase

topics.name: Simple Harmonic Motion: Velocity, Acceleration, and the SHM Differential Equation
topics.summary: A particle executes simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement and always directed toward the mean position: \( a=-\omega^{2}x \). The negative sign is essential, because it makes the force restoring; with a positive sign the particle would run away instead of oscillating. Equivalently, the motion obeys the differential equation \( \dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+\omega^{2}x=0 \), whose solution is \( x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi) \). Differentiating gives the velocity \( v=A\omega\cos(\omega t+\phi) \), which in terms of position is \( v=\omega\sqrt{A^{2}-x^{2}} \). The speed is maximum, \( v_{max}=A\omega \), at the mean position, and zero at the extremes. The acceleration behaves in exactly the opposite way: zero at the mean position and maximum, \( a_{max}=A\omega^{2} \), at the extremes. Velocity leads displacement in phase by \( \pi/2 \), and acceleration is always opposite to displacement, a phase difference of \( \pi \). Dividing \( a_{max} \) by \( v_{max} \) gives \( \omega \) directly.
topics.worked_example:
A particle in SHM has amplitude 5 cm and \( \omega=2 \) rad/s. Find its speed and acceleration at \( x=+3 \) cm.

\( v=2\sqrt{25-9}=8 \) cm/s.

\( a=-\omega^{2}x=-4\times3=-12\ \text{cm/s}^2 \), pointing toward the mean position.
common_mistakes: Placing the maximum speed at the extremes or the maximum acceleration at the mean position
Dropping the negative sign in \( a=-\omega^{2}x \)
Using \( \omega \) instead of \( \omega^{2} \) for acceleration
Reading the coefficient \( \omega^{2} \) in the differential equation as \( \omega \)

topics.name: Energy in Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.summary: The energy of a particle in SHM keeps changing form between kinetic and potential, but for an undamped oscillator the total never changes. The potential energy at displacement \( x \) is \( PE=\tfrac12kx^{2}=\tfrac12m\omega^{2}x^{2} \): zero at the mean position and maximum at the extremes. The kinetic energy is \( KE=\tfrac12m\omega^{2}(A^{2}-x^{2}) \): maximum at the mean position and zero at the extremes. Their sum is the total energy \( E=\tfrac12kA^{2}=\tfrac12m\omega^{2}A^{2} \), the same at every point, so energy is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Useful splits: at \( x=A/2 \), \( PE=\tfrac14E \) and \( KE=\tfrac34E \); at \( x=A/\sqrt{2} \), the two are equal. Because \( KE \) and \( PE \) depend on \( \cos^{2} \) and \( \sin^{2} \) of \( \omega t \), each oscillates with angular frequency \( 2\omega \), twice the oscillator's own. Averaged over a full cycle, each form holds half the total energy.
topics.worked_example:
A spring of \( k=100 \) N/m oscillates with amplitude 0.2 m. Find KE and PE at \( x=0.1 \) m.

\( E=\tfrac12\times100\times0.04=2 \) J.

\( PE=\tfrac12\times100\times0.01=0.5 \) J, so \( KE=2-0.5=1.5 \) J.
common_mistakes: Swapping where KE and PE are maximum
Claiming the total energy of an undamped oscillator changes with position
Using \( \omega \) instead of \( 2\omega \) for how fast KE or PE oscillates
Treating energy as proportional to \( x \) or \( A \) instead of their squares

topics.name: Time Period of Oscillating Systems: Spring-Mass Systems and the Simple Pendulum
topics.summary: For a mass \( m \) on an ideal spring of force constant \( k \), the restoring force \( -kx \) gives \( \omega=\sqrt{k/m} \) and period \( T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k} \): a heavier mass or a softer spring oscillates more slowly. For a simple pendulum of length \( L \) under the small-angle approximation, the restoring acceleration is \( -(g/L)x \), so \( T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g} \). This formula has no mass term at all, because both the restoring force and the inertia scale with the bob's mass; for small angles it is also independent of amplitude. When two springs are combined, the rules are the reverse of those for resistors. In series the effective spring is softer, \( \dfrac{1}{k_{eff}}=\dfrac{1}{k_{1}}+\dfrac{1}{k_{2}} \), giving a longer period; in parallel it is stiffer, \( k_{eff}=k_{1}+k_{2} \), giving a shorter period. Cutting a spring in half doubles the stiffness of each half. For a vertical spring, the equilibrium stretch \( d \) satisfies \( kd=mg \), so \( T=2\pi\sqrt{d/g} \).
topics.worked_example:
Two identical springs of 8 N/m each are joined in series and carry a 1 kg mass. Find the period.

\( k_{eff}=\dfrac{8\times8}{16}=4 \) N/m.

\( T=2\pi\sqrt{1/4}=\pi \) s. (In parallel, \( k_{eff}=16 \) N/m would give \( \pi/2 \) s.)
common_mistakes: Inserting the bob's mass into the pendulum period
Using the pendulum formula's mass-independence for a spring, whose period does depend on mass
Borrowing resistor rules: adding spring constants in series
Forgetting the square root when scaling \( T \) with \( m \), \( k \), \( L \) or \( g \)

topics.name: Damped Oscillations, Forced Oscillations, and Resonance
topics.summary: Real oscillators lose energy to their surroundings. A damping force, usually taken proportional to velocity, \( F_{d}=-bv \), makes the equation of motion \( m\dfrac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}=-kx-bv \). The result is damped oscillation: the amplitude decays with time, \( A(t)=A_{0}e^{-bt/(2m)} \), while the lost mechanical energy appears as heat in the medium. Since energy goes as \( A^{2} \), it decays twice as fast in the exponent, \( E=E_{0}e^{-bt/m} \). For light damping the frequency is only slightly less than the natural value \( \omega_{0}=\sqrt{k/m} \). When a periodic external force drives the system, it eventually oscillates at the driving frequency \( \omega_{d} \), not its natural one, with a steady amplitude set by the balance between energy fed in and energy lost. The amplitude is largest when \( \omega_{d} \) is close to \( \omega_{0} \): this is resonance. Less damping gives a taller, sharper resonance peak. Swings, radio tuning, bridges under marching soldiers and car suspensions are everyday examples.
topics.worked_example:
A damped oscillator has \( m=0.5 \) kg and \( b=0.1 \) kg/s. When does its amplitude fall to \( A_{0}/e \)?

Set \( bt/(2m)=1 \): \( t=2m/b=10 \) s.

Its energy is then \( E_{0}/e^{2} \).
common_mistakes: Thinking a forced oscillator settles at its natural frequency rather than the driving frequency
Believing more damping makes the resonance peak taller
Forgetting that energy falls as the square of amplitude
Mixing up the amplitude time \( 2m/b \) with the energy time \( m/b \)

questions.topic: Periodic and Oscillatory Motion: Displacement as a Function of Time
questions.question: Which of the following motions is periodic but NOT oscillatory?
options: The revolution of the Earth around the Sun
A simple pendulum swinging about its lowest point
A mass on a spring bouncing up and down
questions.explanation:
Periodic motion repeats itself after equal intervals of time; oscillatory motion is periodic motion that goes to and fro about a mean position.

The Earth returns to the same point in its orbit every year, so the motion is periodic, but it never moves back and forth about a mean position.

Pendulums, springs, and strings all move to and fro, so they are oscillatory.
questions.hint: Ask whether the object moves back and forth about a fixed mean position.

A spring-mass system moves back and forth about its equilibrium point, so it is oscillatory
A vibrating string moves to and fro about its rest position, so it is oscillatory

Series: \( \dfrac{1}{k_{eff}}=\dfrac16+\dfrac13=\dfrac12 \), so \( k_{eff}=2 \) N/m.

\( E=\tfrac12\times2\times(0.2)^{2}=0.04 \) J.
questions.hint: Series springs give a smaller \( k_{eff} \).
distractor_logic: Uses the parallel value \( k_{eff}=9 \) N/m, borrowing the resistor rule for series
Forgets the factor of one half
Forgets to square the amplitude

questions.question: As a damped oscillator's amplitude decreases cycle by cycle, the speed with which it passes through the mean position
options: increases from one pass to the next
stays the same on every pass
decreases from one pass to the next
questions.explanation:
Maximum speed is \( A\omega \), reached at the mean position.

Damping reduces \( A \), so each pass through the mean position is slower.
questions.hint: Maximum speed is proportional to amplitude.
distractor_logic: Energy is being lost, so the maximum speed cannot grow
Maximum speed \( A\omega \) falls as \( A \) falls
The speed is maximum, not zero, at the mean position

questions.topic: Periodic and Oscillatory Motion: Displacement as a Function of Time
questions.question: A simple pendulum of length 1 m, at a place where \( g=\pi^{2}\ \text{m/s}^2 \), is released from rest at an angular displacement \( \theta=0.1 \) rad at \( t=0 \). What is its angular displacement at \( t=1 \) s?
questions.explanation:
\( T=2\pi\sqrt{1/\pi^{2}}=2 \) s, so \( \omega=\pi \) rad/s and \( \theta=0.1\cos(\pi t) \).

At \( t=1 \) s: \( \theta=0.1\cos\pi=-0.1 \) rad, the opposite extreme.
questions.hint: Find the period first; 1 s is what fraction of it?
distractor_logic: After one full period it would be back at \( +0.1 \) rad, but 1 s is only half the 2 s period
The lowest point is reached at \( T/4=0.5 \) s
Takes half the amplitude, as if \( \cos\pi \) were \( -\tfrac12 \)

questions.question: A spring-mass system with total energy 2 J, force constant 400 N/m, and mass 1 kg oscillates. What is its maximum speed?
questions.explanation:
All energy is kinetic at the mean position: \( \tfrac12mv_{max}^{2}=2 \).

\( v_{max}=\sqrt{4}=2 \) m/s (check: \( A=0.1 \) m, \( \omega=20 \) rad/s, \( A\omega=2 \) m/s).
questions.hint: All energy is kinetic at the mean position.
distractor_logic: 40 is \( A\omega^{2} \), the maximum acceleration in \( \text{m/s}^2 \)
Forgets the factor of 2 in \( v=\sqrt{2E/m} \)
Computes \( 2E/m \) but forgets the square root
